newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: SAFRICA SAPREF PLANS REFINERY UPGRADE.
newsitem.headline: SAFRICA SAPREF PLANS REFINERY UPGRADE.

text.p: The South African Petroleum Refinery (Pty) Ltd (Sapref) said on Friday it planned a 200 million rand two-year upgrade and centralisation of control systems at its Durban oil refinery.

The refinery, a joint venture between British Petroleum Plc and the Royal Dutch/Shell group, was also weighing whether to undertake a much bigger investment aimed at boosting production to meet fast-growing demand for products, especially gasoline.
Managing director Peter Fransen said the initial 200 million rand upgrade would boost throughout at the country's largest refinery marginally, and would not disrupt production.
"We are not shutting down for this purpose because the new electronic controls will be installed parallel to the existing pneumatic controls," Fransen told a news briefing.
The project is over and above the 50 million to 100 million rand spent on the refinery annually to effect small plant changes aimed at keeping it abreast of technology, he said.
The project, which will have a 70 percent local content and be completed in 1998, will boost throughput of the 165,000 barrels per day plant by one or two percent, Fransen said.

"The project will increase the yield of high value refined products from imported crude oil, improve energy efficiencies and improve environmental performance, thereby reducing the quantity of imported petroleum products," he said.
Fransen said the upgrade would equip the largest refinery in Africa for any future expansion programmes.

Sapref recently finished a master plan study into the expansion of the Durban plant which in its first phase could include an additional crude unit and a platformer which is used to boost the octane of petrol, he said.

"Shell and BP Sapref are studying in close cooperation with both shareholders investment options to meet the growing demands in South Africa and surrounding countries for transport fuels, particularly gasoline and jet," he said.
A final investment decision to go forward with the $250 to $350 million project could be expected early in 1998.
The refinery's last major upgrade was in 1993 when a new crude distillation project was completed at a cost of 415 million rand.
Last year the instrumentation at Sapref's lubricants plant was modernised at a cost of 39 million rand.
BP Africa managing director John Greensmith said earlier this month South Africa could run out of gasoline refining capacity as early as this year, forcing imports.

The country's oil industry has long debated the need for additional capacity, but oil companies have been reluctant to commit themselves pending clarification of plans to liberalise the domestic oil market.
